law_discussed: ICT Act 2006; DSA 2018; Pornography Control Act 2012
key_findings: Sub-inspectors face internal barriers (little tech/logistics at station level, shallow cyber training, non-investigative duty load) and external ones (victim non-cooperation from shame, bKash and Facebook slow or refusing to share data, SIMs registered on others' NIDs, volatile digital evidence, cross-jurisdiction offenders).
prevalence_reported: Cites Dhaka Cyber Tribunal 2013-2020: 2,669 cases, 768 disposed, 22 convictions (2.86%); ~80% of victims unsatisfied with police (CCAF 2023) - secondary figures
author_gaps: Perspective of specialised units and victims not covered; small convenience sample
recommendations: Station-level cyber tools; cyber/digital-forensics modules in Sardah training; regular in-service training; staffing; police-private sector (MFS, platform) cooperation; curb fraudulent SIM registration
quality_note: Small sample (n=8), all male SIs, two districts; clear methods; author is criminologist (PhD on cyber violence victimisation) - possible supervisor/collaborator contact

key_findings: Curated ~50k Bangla/English/Banglish SMS (fraud vs legitimate, from Facebook scam reports and volunteers); Bangla-BERT-base best (91% accuracy, recall 100%, precision 85.5%); prototype app shows pop-up scam warnings.
author_gaps: No public Bangla fraud-SMS dataset existed; no formal user testing of alerts
recommendations: Integrate into telecom/MFS SMS filtering
quality_note: Internal inconsistencies (conclusion describes emotion detection; recall 100% for all models implausible); technical only

population: university students; police or justice actors
theory: none (trust in automation / appropriate reliance framing)
key_findings: 77% cautious about treating digital media as authentic, 64% say legal professionals need stronger deepfake-evaluation skills, 56% aware AI can fabricate media; awareness weakly/not associated with endorsing training. Argues provenance, authentication and evidentiary weight should be trained separately (Evidence Act ss 65A-65B).
author_gaps: No measure of actual detection skill; non-probability sample dominated by law students; test practitioners with case tasks; pre-post training evaluation
recommendations: Case-based legal training on provenance, preservation and interpreting forensic reports
quality_note: Same 'Group 6' dataset used in companion papers (R0022 likely) - not independent; GenAI-assisted drafting disclosed; careful statistics

key_findings: 49% recognised AI misuse for phishing/impersonation, 81% verify unusual requests, 82% use security practices; awareness not associated with protective behaviour after adjustment, daily AI use was.
author_gaps: Need validated measures and behavioural (not self-report) outcomes; prospective designs
recommendations: Distinguish recognition, detection confidence and behaviour in university cyber education
quality_note: Same 'Group 6' dataset as R0015 - not independent sample

key_findings: XGBoost best on synthetic PaySim mobile-money data (F1 0.54, PR-AUC 0.57); calibration and SHAP explanations; top-1% adaptive alerting cuts false positives 39% but halves recall.
author_gaps: No real Bangladeshi MFS/bank transaction data available; validation on governed local data needed
recommendations: Bangladesh Bank e-KYC guidance should encourage chronological validation and explainable, capacity-aware alerting
quality_note: Uses NO Bangladesh data - evidence of data-access gap for MFS fraud research

key_findings: CSA 2026's vague offences ('defamatory online content', 'false information', 'cyber propaganda', 'cyber terrorism') fail ICCPR Art 19(3) legality/necessity/proportionality; ss 31-36 allow device/traffic access without judicial warrant; chilling effect; compared with US First Amendment, EU DSA and Shreya Singhal (India). Fails all five tests for sound cyber legislation.
recommendations: Five reform principles: narrow definitions, judicial warrants, proportionate penalties, independent oversight, decriminalise defamation
quality_note: Undergraduate-authored; low-tier journal (IRE); some garbled text

key_findings: Bangladesh lacks treaty networks (not party to Budapest Convention), relies on slow MLATs, has outdated digital-evidence and data-access procedures; compared with US CLOUD Act and EU EIO/e-Evidence, causing investigative delays in transnational cases (e.g. 2016 Bangladesh Bank heist).
recommendations: Harmonised cybercrime definitions; streamlined MLATs; digital evidence reform; capacity building; accede to Budapest Convention
quality_note: Secondary sources only

location: national (comparative: EU, Italy, UK, US, China, S Korea, India, Bangladesh)
law_discussed: CSA 2026 / Ordinance 2025 (as coded in index); Pornography Control Act 2012
key_findings: Leximetric Synthetic Media Legal Coverage Index: Bangladesh scored lowest (6/18, 33%) vs US 15/18; sexual-deepfake offences widely covered, likeness/licensing rights least. Proposes four-layer model (right, licence, transparency, liability) for Bangladesh.
recommendations: Dignity-based personality right with copyright as enforcement container; transparency and platform duties
quality_note: Author based in India; journal (Int J Special Education) off-topic outlet; Bangladesh is one of 8 cases but scored and targeted by recommendations

key_findings: 2017 India-Bangladesh CERT MoU (CERT-In / BGD e-GOV CIRT) is weak because Art 5 defers to divergent national laws; no binding standards, oversight or law-enforcement integration. Proposes AI tools for harmonisation and joint threat intelligence.
prevalence_reported: Cites secondary figures: DMP 2023 23.9% of cyber cases Facebook breaches/extortion/fraud; '73% of Bangladeshi women experienced cybercrime' (unsourced)
recommendations: Operationalise MoU Art 5 with joint protocols, cyber exercises, shared AI-based threat classification and evidence standards
quality_note: Indian political science author; low-tier journal; largely descriptive, weakly sourced statistics

key_findings: DSA 2018 (and Nigeria's Cybercrimes Act 2015) use vague offences ('false', 'offensive', 'defamatory') enabling selective enforcement against journalists/activists; misinformation used to justify censorship; opaque state-platform takedowns; Bangladesh enforcement more centralised and systematic than Nigeria's.
author_gaps: Desk-based; no interviews or enforcement data
recommendations: Narrow definitions; independent multi-stakeholder digital regulator; platform transparency; media literacy over punishment; rights-based data protection
quality_note: Nigerian ICT agency authors; several references look unverifiable (possible fabricated citations); secondary sources only

key_findings: 55% see AI misuse as 'very common', women and children seen as most vulnerable; 65% think current laws inadequate for AI harms; two deepfake harassment/blackmail cases show barriers to justice. Calls AI harms a 'legal response gap'.
recommendations: Victim-centred legal reform, digital forensic capacity, AI liability rules, AI governance framework, digital literacy
quality_note: Perception survey (not victimisation); sampling not specified; low-tier journal

key_findings: Three forms: identity-based (body shaming, gender-nonconforming students labelled, regional accents), interactional aggression (sarcasm, exclusion of high achievers), technologically mediated manipulation (fake profiles sending fake nudes to family, deepfakes, doxing, strategic tagging). Memes/GIFs/emojis disguise hostility as humour. Most victims never report (fear of retaliation, privacy, futility).
author_gaps: Quantitative measurement of instances and impacts needed
recommendations: Anonymous campus reporting, anti-retaliation policy, peer support, teacher training, disciplinary action
quality_note: Good qualitative victim data; linguistics not criminology; purposive sample

key_findings: CSA 2026 lacks clear definitions and an ethical basis for AI-driven defamation/deepfakes; proposes codifying digital defamation via Islamic principles (Hifz al-Ird), discretionary (ta'zir) restorative punishment, and protecting sincere political criticism (nasiha).
recommendations: Shariah-informed definitions of digital defamation; restorative justice for deepfake victims; protect constructive criticism
quality_note: Written in Bangla (legacy SutonnyMJ font, text garbled in extraction); Islamic Studies authors; normative

key_findings: Lists attacks on Bangladeshi critical infrastructure (Sonali Bank 2013, Bangladesh Bank 2016, BPDB 2015, WannaCry at BERC 2017, DESCO prepaid-meter hack of 18,000 meters, Biman ransomware, Standard Chartered card fraud 2025); incidents under-reported and opaque. Compares US/UK/EU public-private partnership models.
recommendations: National Cyber Security Commission; PPP information sharing; transparent incident reporting; awareness campaigns
quality_note: Borderline (infrastructure security more than crime); relies heavily on one newspaper source (Wahid 2025); literature-only

key_findings: Mainly physical, psychological and financial COVID-era safety; DSA appears only briefly (one interviewee quote; cites Article 19: 60 DSA cases against 100 people incl. 22 journalists in Jan-May 2020).
prevalence_reported: Secondary: Article 19 2020 - 60 DSA cases, 100 people, 22 journalists
recommendations: nr
quality_note: Excluded at full text: DSA is a minor theme. Article 19 figure useful as background

key_findings: Digital evidence in general (Evidence (Amendment) Act 2022 s65B) assessed against Islamic evidentiary principles; proposes Shariah-Compliant Digital Evidence Framework. Not tied to cybercrime cases.
author_gaps: Empirical study of digital evidence use in courts; deepfake identification
recommendations: nr
quality_note: Excluded at full text: digital evidence in general, not cybercrime (per rule)

key_findings: All defamation is criminal in Bangladesh with no public/private figure distinction; DSA online defamation provisions allowed warrantless arrest and device seizure and were used against journalists, academics and opponents (many cases 2020-21), chilling debate.
recommendations: Decriminalise defamation; serious-harm threshold; public-figure 'actual malice' doctrine
quality_note: Dhaka University Law Journal (reputable domestic)

location: Bogura; Rangpur; Natore; Sirajganj; Jamalpur; Rajshahi
key_findings: Delivery fraud against sellers (fake cash-on-delivery orders, refusals, fake returns) was the most consistent harm reported by all rural women F-commerce sellers; losses borne entirely by seller, no recourse against buyer or courier; coping = advance payment, blocking. Online harassment mainly from male customers adds emotional stress and triggers household suspicion; bKash/Nagad accounts often controlled by male relatives.
author_gaps: Urban-rural comparison; quantitative impact studies; platform algorithm effects
recommendations: Grievance redress for delivery fraud with couriers/platforms; Meta scam-profile warnings and reporting; collateral-free credit; digital rights training
quality_note: Seller-side fraud victimisation is rarely studied - useful gap evidence

key_findings: Comparative policy analysis on 5 dimensions; Bangladesh's NCSS 2023 judged more operationally detailed than Pakistan's 2021 NCSP (cybercrime units, reporting portal, MLATs); Pakistan's PECA criticised as speech-focused; both lack victim protection for individuals and e-commerce users.
recommendations: Funded research agenda, PPP mechanisms, curriculum integration, victim protection (directed at Pakistan)
quality_note: Pakistani author; treats Bangladesh mainly as benchmark; some claims about Bangladesh (e.g. MLAT partnerships) contradict R0039 - descriptive, uncritical of DSA

key_findings: Nationally representative: 6.6% of adolescents reported cyberbullying (verbal 31.6%, physical 20.8%); cyberbullying independently associated with higher depressive symptoms (b=1.15, p=0.012); cumulative bullying exposure shows graded association. No significant gender interaction for cyberbullying.
prevalence_reported: Cyberbullying victimisation 6.60% among 15-19 year olds (BAHWS 2019-20, n=9,116) - contrasts with ~32% in small convenience samples
recommendations: Comprehensive bullying prevention including online; accessible psychosocial services
quality_note: KEY PAPER: only nationally representative cyber-victimisation estimate so far; PLOS Mental Health; secondary analysis of public dataset (BAHWS) - usable for PhD
